evidence: Cic. de Or. 1.228: quod pūpillum fīlium ipse paene in umerōs suōs extulisset (Lewis & Short s.v. umerus)
Cic. Sen. 33: cum umerīs sustinēret bovem (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: An ordinary description: Traupman and Morgan–Owens have no word for carrying a child on one’s shoulders. Cicero has in umerōs efferre, to lift onto one’s shoulders, and umerīs sustinēre, to bear on them; to ride there is in umerīs vehī.

phrases.latin: Theodōrus autem, in umerīs ejus vectus, bacillum aduncum tenēns
phrases.english: Theo, riding on his shoulders and holding his hooked stick

sources: Theodōrus et pater · Ad Larem avītum, Libellī I–VII, as they stood on 7 November 2026, with their glosses. Examples marked “Libellus” quote those texts word for word; classical passages are cited by author.
